title: Start here: what are we trying to establish?
intro: Begin with Shoham’s distinction between research questions. Then use the risk taxonomy to connect those questions to the design and evaluation of interacting AI systems. The same observation can support different claims, depending on the model and the evidence available.

title: Open-source game theory and commitment
question: When can visible, conditional commitments change the outcome of an interaction?
intro: Start with programs that can inspect one another, then compare proof-based, simulation-based, and similarity-based routes to cooperation. Keep the informational and computational assumptions in view. A commitment that helps in one interaction can create a race or conflict in another. For the schedule’s question about safe Pareto improvements, specify the baseline and the conditions under which a proposed modification leaves every participant no worse off.
connection: Schedule Part I and the opening game

title: Stochastic dynamics of multi-agent learning
question: How do interacting learners change over time, and when are the approximations informative?
intro: Use the textbook to establish the objects being modeled, then read Chu and Geng together. The first technical question is what pair information adds to an aggregate population model; the second is when a separation of timescales simplifies the learning dynamics. Lanctot’s PSRO paper appears in Collection IV, where it connects learning to strategy exploration.

title: Multi-agent AI control
question: What does a control evaluation establish under its threat model?
intro: Read the original control paper for the evaluation setup, then the untrusted-monitoring paper for the collusion problem at the center of Morgan Sinclaire’s talk. The formal game and safety-case readings help expose the assumptions connecting an experiment to a deployment claim.

groups.title: Monitoring when the model may subvert the protocol

title: Empirical game-theoretic analysis
question: What does an equilibrium of a measured, restricted game tell us about the underlying interaction?
intro: Follow the loop from simulator to payoffs to strategic analysis, then back to the search for new policies. There are two distinct gaps: uncertainty in the entries you estimated, and profitable strategies that the game does not yet represent. The supplied slides and worksheet use Wellman’s survey as their main source.
connection: Schedule Part IV and the EGTA exercises

title: Normative agency, beliefs, and goals
question: What structure can an optimal policy have, and what does that tell us about an implemented agent?
intro: Begin with Rosas’s essay, then use the technical references to separate belief-state sufficiency from stronger separation claims. Keep existence, optimality, and implementation distinct: a useful mathematical representation is not by itself an empirical explanation of a trained system.
connection: The schedule bibliography’s “Part IV (normative agency)” · retained here as a separate collection

title: Descriptive explanations and collective agency
question: Which mechanisms could explain apparent altruism, and what evidence distinguishes them?
intro: Read the incident reports before the explanatory essays. Then compare evolutionary, representational, and collective-agent accounts without assuming that only one can be involved. The useful output is a set of discriminating predictions and interventions, with their assumptions stated.
connection: Schedule Part V, small-group discussion, and closing
